stories.title: The man with the golden touch: James Bond franchise is a money-spinner
summary: Big-screen debut of Ian Fleming’s creation in 1962, with Sean Connery as lead in Dr No, was start of marketing dreamNew James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert PattinsonShare your thoughts on the castingPeter Bradshaw’s takeRobert Pattinson’s journey to James BondJames Bond may be 73 years old but the superspy holds a licence to print money, at the centre of an evergreen multibillion-pound franchise spanning blockbuster films, merchandise, licensing deals and sponsorship.The announcement that the Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson is the next Bond comes seven years after Daniel Craig revealed that No Time To Die would be his last outing as 007.

stories.title: 'Parents are offering to pay kids' wages': Salon owner
summary: National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, according to a new report from former government minister Alan Milburn, due to be published on Tuesday.

stories.title: Several companies are using Trump tariff refunds for corporate bonuses
summary: Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found.After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership.

summary: Some parents are so desperate for their children to find a job that they've offered to pay their wages, one hairdresser has told the BBC.

stories.title: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
summary: Surge in prices is forcing many to cut back on spending, with a projected 21% increase in costs of those householdsMillions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases.
